scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In the kratons of Yogyakarta and Surakarta, dance is treated as a 'pusaka'—a sacred heirloom that functions as a tool for moral education and self-reflection rather than mere entertainment.
This is Javanese dance. Ancient to present.
on_screen: Title card: Javanese dance · Indonesia · Ancient to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Javanese dance is heavily influenced by the Hindu-Buddhist legacy of Indonesia, with many of its stories and costumes derived from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
The tradition was fostered and codified within the Javanese Kratons, particularly the Yogyakarta Sultanate and Surakarta Sunanate, which remain the centers of the Mataram culture.
These dances are considered sacred heirlooms (pusaka) passed down from palace ancestors.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dance serves multiple roles: royal entertainment, courtship, military training, and moral education.
Sacred court dances like Bedhaya are performed for significant royal events.
Commoner dances are used for celebrations, social gatherings, and rituals like Reog.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Kebyar Cosmic Dance To Phil Morton And The Javanese People (https://archive.org/details/kebyar__cosmic__dance)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The movement is characterized by deliberate, slow, and controlled gestures.
Courtly styles require intense discipline to master specific body and hand gestures.
Men's dances (Beksan putra) range from martial drills to narrative roles, while women's dances (Beksan putri) focus on subtle, precise staging.
Watch for Alus, Gagah.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Distinct staging with subtle layers of meaning; often symmetrical in court rituals.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The Gamelan orchestra is a prerequisite for Javanese dance.
The music provides the rhythmic structure that dictates the slow, graceful pace of the performers.
Listen for the Gamelan orchestra, Gong, Kendhang (drum), Saron.
The pulse is Colotomic cycles (Gamelan structure).
A shimmering, metallic texture created by bronze percussion, characterized by slow, expansive cycles and sudden shifts in tempo led by the drum.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Interlocking patterns of gongs, kempul, and kenong.
scenes.music: the music brief's underscore at its own tempo; drop narration under the hook of a verified recording if licensed, else original

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes and jewelry often reflect the Hindu epic tales of the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
Court dances are typically performed within the 'pendopo' (open pavilions) of the royal palaces, while commoner dances take place in village squares or city streets.
Commoner dances like Kuda Lumping may involve props like woven bamboo horses.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Javanese Sultans of Yogyakarta and Surakarta are historically recognized as the primary patrons and creators of the courtly dance forms.
The two main streams are the courtly traditions of Yogyakarta and Surakarta.
Javanese dance is a subclass of Indonesian dance, distinct from Balinese and Sundanese styles.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Javanese dance is sibling of Balinese dance: Contrasts Javanese refinement with vigorous and expressive movements.
Javanese dance is sibling of Sundanese dance: Contrasts Javanese introspection with cheerful and sensual qualities.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Certain court dances are considered 'pusaka' (sacred heirlooms) and are performed as meditative rituals for moral education and spiritual reflection within the palace context.
